p: Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight we travel back a very long way, before anybody wrote down a single number. I want you to see that counting is older than writing, older than cities, and perhaps one of the oldest things our minds do.

Our road map: first, notched bones. Second, clay tokens in ancient Mesopotamia. Third, the Babylonians and their curious love of sixty. And fourth, a very English story about tally sticks, which ends in flames.
## Notches on bone

In 1950, in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo, a Belgian geologist found a small bone, the Ishango bone, with groups of notches cut along it. It is perhaps twenty thousand years old. Scholars still argue about what the notches mean. Some see a tally, some a calendar, and some think they see prime numbers, though I would not put my umbrella on that last one. But somebody was counting something.
Even older is the Lebombo bone, from the mountains between South Africa and Eswatini, a baboon's leg bone with twenty-nine notches, over forty thousand years old.
A tally is the simplest kind of counting. One mark for one thing. One sheep, one notch. You do not need a word for seventeen. You just need seventeen notches, and the patience of a shepherd.

?? Here is a little puzzle. A shepherd makes one notch for every sheep that leaves the fold in the morning. How can he tell, in the evening, whether any are missing, without knowing any number words at all?

=> He runs his finger along the notches as each sheep comes home, one notch for each sheep. If there are notches left over, sheep are missing. That is matching one thing to another, and it is the very heart of counting.
## Clay tokens

Move forward to Mesopotamia, the land between the rivers Tigris and Euphrates, in what is now Iraq. From around eight thousand years before Christ, people there used small clay tokens: little cones, spheres and discs, each standing for a measure of grain, a sheep, or a jar of oil.

The archaeologist Denise Schmandt-Besserat argued that these tokens led to writing itself. Traders sealed tokens inside hollow clay balls, so that nobody could tamper with the count. But then you had to break the ball to check. So they pressed the tokens into the outside of the soft clay before sealing it, leaving a picture of what was inside. And then somebody had the bright idea: why bother with the tokens at all? Just press the marks into clay. That, very roughly, is how numbers came to be written, and perhaps how writing began.
## The Babylonians and sixty

By about four thousand years ago, the Babylonians had a remarkable system of numbers. They wrote with a reed on wet clay, making little wedge-shaped marks called cuneiform. And they counted not in tens, as we do, but in sixties.

Why sixty? Nobody knows for certain. But sixty is a wonderfully obliging number. You can share sixty things equally among two, three, four, five, six, ten, twelve, fifteen, twenty or thirty people. Ten, by comparison, splits only into twos and fives. Mrs Blewitt says any number that divides by three is a friend to anyone who has ever cut a cake.

We still live with the Babylonians every day. Sixty seconds in a minute. Sixty minutes in an hour. Three hundred and sixty degrees in a circle. Every time you look at a clock, you are reading Babylonian arithmetic.

They were not merely counting sheep, either. A clay tablet now in New York, called Plimpton 322, written around 1800 before Christ, contains a table of numbers related to right-angled triangles, more than a thousand years before Pythagoras was born.
?? A quick one while I pour. How many minutes are there in two and a half hours?
=> One hundred and fifty. Two hours is one hundred and twenty minutes, and half an hour is thirty more.
## The tally sticks of the Exchequer

Now to England, and a story I love. For centuries the royal Exchequer, the government's treasury, recorded money on tally sticks. A stick of hazel or willow was notched to show a sum: a broad notch for a thousand pounds, a narrower one for a hundred, and so on. Then the stick was split down its length. Each party kept one half. The halves could only fit together with each other, so nobody could cheat by adding a notch. The larger piece, the stock, went to the person who had lent the money, which some say is where we get the word stockholder.

The system lasted, remarkably, until 1826. Then the government decided it had a great many old sticks to dispose of. On the sixteenth of October 1834 they were burned in a furnace beneath the House of Lords. The furnace was overloaded, the chimneys overheated, and by evening the old Palace of Westminster was ablaze. Crowds gathered along the Thames to watch. The painter Turner was there, sketching. The Houses of Parliament you know today, with the great clock tower, were built to replace what burned. Mr Charles Dickens later made much of the story in a speech, as an example of official foolishness.
I was five years old at the time, in Bristol, and I confess I do not remember it. But I like to think that the old way of counting went out in a blaze of glory.
## Summary

Let us gather up what we learned. People counted long before they wrote, by matching one thing to another: notches, pebbles, tokens. Written numbers may have grown from clay tokens in Mesopotamia. The Babylonians counted in sixties, which is why our clocks and circles are as they are. And England kept its accounts on notched sticks until 1826, and burned the Palace of Westminster getting rid of them.

Next time, we shall meet the great idea that made our own numbers possible: place value, the secret of why the same digit can mean two, or twenty, or two hundred. Until then, my dear friend, keep warm, and keep away from overloaded furnaces.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight a story of travel: the long journey of nothing. Zero is the only number that needed a passport. It crossed deserts, changed its name several times, and was once banned by the bankers of Florence.
Our road map: first, zero as a placeholder in Babylon. Second, zero as a real number in India. Third, the journey through Baghdad. And fourth, its arrival in Europe and the suspicion it met there.
## A gap in Babylon

Last time we saw how place value needs a way to say "nothing in this place". The Babylonians, with their numbers in sixties, managed for centuries without one. They simply left a small gap, and hoped the reader noticed. Imagine reading accounts where everything depended on the width of a space.

By about three hundred years before Christ, Babylonian scribes began using a sign, two slanted wedges, to mark an empty place. But it was only a placeholder. Nobody thought of it as a number you could add or multiply. Far away and independently, the Maya of Central America also invented a zero for their calendars, often drawn as a shell.
## A number in its own right: India

The great leap happened in India. Indian mathematicians used a place-value system with ten digits, the ancestor of ours, and they wrote zero as a dot or a small circle. They called it shunya, meaning empty.

In the year 628 the astronomer Brahmagupta wrote a book called the Brahmasphutasiddhanta, and in it he did something wonderful. He treated zero as a number with rules of its own. A number plus zero is the number. A number minus zero is the number. A number times zero is zero. He also wrote rules for what he called debts and fortunes, which we would call negative and positive numbers.

In plain words: adding nothing changes nothing, and five lots of nothing is still nothing. Brahmagupta also tried to say what happens when you divide by zero, and there, I am afraid, he went astray: he said that zero divided by zero is zero. Mathematicians now say that dividing by zero has no meaning at all. But do not think less of him. He was the first to try, and the first to try is always braver than the second.
There is a temple at Gwalior in India with an inscription from the year 876 that includes a zero, a little round circle in the number 270. Visitors can still see it.
?? A small question while I find the biscuits. What is seven times zero, and what is seven plus zero?
=> Seven times zero is zero. Seven plus zero is seven. Zero has no effect when you add it, and swallows everything when you multiply by it.
## The road through Baghdad

The Indian numerals travelled west. In Baghdad, in the early ninth century, there was a great centre of learning called the House of Wisdom. There the Persian scholar Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi wrote a book on calculating with the Indian numerals. His own name, written in Latin as Algoritmi, gave us our word algorithm. Another of his books, on solving equations, had al-jabr in its title, and gave us the word algebra. We shall meet him again in the foothills.

The Arabic word for zero was sifr, meaning empty. When it reached Europe in Latin it became zephirum, then in Italian zefiro, and at last zero. The same word sifr also became cipher, which for a long time meant zero, and later came to mean a secret code. So a cipher is, by origin, a nothing. I find that rather poetic.
## Arrival in Europe

In 1202 a young man from Pisa, Leonardo, whom we call Fibonacci, published a book called Liber Abaci, the Book of Calculation. As a boy he had travelled to North Africa with his father, a merchant, and learned the Indian numerals there. He saw at once how much easier they made the arithmetic of trade, and he wrote his book to show the merchants of Italy.

The merchants were not all grateful. These new numerals were easy to forge. A zero can be turned into a six or a nine with a stroke of the pen, whereas Roman numerals are harder to tamper with. In 1299 the bankers' guild of Florence, so the records tell us, ordered its members to write sums in Roman numerals or in words, not in the new figures. It took a few centuries for suspicion to fade.
My Aunt Hester, as I have mentioned, also distrusted zero. When I told her it had been banned in Florence she said that showed great good sense on the part of the Florentines.
?? Here is one to think about. Why would a zero be easy to forge into a six or a nine?

=> Because a zero is a simple loop. Add a stroke to the top and you have a six; add a tail and you have a nine. That is one reason bankers liked to write amounts in words as well, as we still do on cheques.
## Summary

Zero began as a gap, became a placeholder in Babylon, and became a true number in India, where Brahmagupta wrote down its rules in 628. It travelled through Baghdad, where al-Khwarizmi's books spread the Indian numerals and gave us the words algorithm and algebra. Fibonacci brought it to Europe in 1202, and after some suspicion, it conquered the world.
Next time, we turn from history to practice, with a lecture on the art of making ten, the first trick of mental arithmetic. Until then, my dear friend, think kindly of nothing.

Good evening, my dear friend. Pull your chair nearer the fire. Tonight there is no algebra to learn, only a story, and it is one of my favourites, because it happened in my own London, among people whose names were in the newspapers of my youth. It is the story of a mathematician who wished to make machines think in numbers, and of the young woman who understood him better than anyone.

Before I begin, an honest word. I never met either of them. I have read their writings, and the reading ticket to the library of the future, which I hold by some arrangement I do not pretend to understand, has let me read what historians since have discovered. What follows is the history as it is established, and where a story is doubtful, I shall say so.
## Mr Babbage and the tables
Charles Babbage was born in London in 1791. He was a Cambridge man, like me, though rather grander: from 1828 to 1839 he held the Lucasian chair of mathematics, the chair Isaac Newton had once held.

In Babbage's day, calculations for navigation, astronomy, insurance and engineering relied on printed tables: books of logarithms, of tides, of the positions of stars. They were computed by hand, by people called computers, for that was then a job title, not a machine. And they were full of errors. A wrong figure in a navigation table could put a ship on the rocks.

So the story goes, and it rests on Babbage's own later account, he was checking such tables with his friend John Herschel and exclaimed that he wished they had been calculated by steam. Whether the words were exactly those, I would not swear in court. But the wish was real.
## The Difference Engine

Babbage's first design, from the early 1820s, was the Difference Engine. It used a clever trick called the method of differences, by which a table of a polynomial can be built using only addition, over and over. Addition is the easiest thing to make a machine do with gear wheels.

Here is the trick in miniature. Take the square numbers: one, four, nine, sixteen, twenty-five. The differences between them are three, five, seven, nine. The differences of those differences are always two. So, starting from the right beginnings, you can produce every square number by repeatedly adding: add two to the difference, add the difference to the square. No multiplication at all. That is what the engine's columns of wheels were to do.
?? While I pour. The next square after twenty-five. The last difference was nine. Add two to get the next difference, then add that to twenty-five.
=> The next difference is eleven, and twenty-five plus eleven is thirty-six. Six squared.

The British Government funded the work, eventually paying around seventeen thousand pounds, an enormous sum. The engineer Joseph Clement made superb parts. But costs rose, Babbage and Clement quarrelled, and by the early 1830s work had stopped. A beautiful finished section of the engine still exists, and it works.
## The Analytical Engine

Babbage, being Babbage, had meanwhile thought of something far greater. From 1834 he designed the Analytical Engine: not a machine for one kind of table, but a general calculating machine that could be instructed to carry out any sequence of operations.

It had a store, where numbers were kept on columns of wheels, and a mill, where arithmetic was done. Instructions were fed in on punched cards, an idea borrowed from the Jacquard loom, which wove complicated patterns in silk by following chains of punched cards. And the engine could make decisions: depending on a result, it could take a different course. With the library ticket I may tell you that these are exactly the essential parts of the computers of your age: memory, processor, program, and the ability to branch.
It was never built. The design was too large, too costly and too far ahead of the workshops of the day.
## Lady Lovelace

Augusta Ada, later Countess of Lovelace, was born in 1815, the daughter of the poet Lord Byron and of Annabella Milbanke, who was so fond of mathematics that Byron called her his Princess of Parallelograms. The parents separated when Ada was a baby, and her mother saw to it that she was thoroughly schooled in mathematics. She later studied by correspondence with Augustus De Morgan, of whom you will hear much more.
Ada met Babbage in 1833, when she was seventeen, and saw a demonstration piece of the Difference Engine. She was fascinated, and they became friends.

In 1842 an Italian engineer, Luigi Menabrea, published in French an account of the Analytical Engine, based on a lecture Babbage had given in Turin. Ada translated it into English, and added her own Notes, labelled A to G. The Notes were longer than the paper itself, nearly three times as long. They were published in 1843.
## Note G

In the last note, Note G, Ada set out in detail how the Engine could calculate the Bernoulli numbers, an important sequence in number theory, laying out the operations step by step in a table. This is often called the first published computer program. Historians argue about how much of the work was hers and how much Babbage's, and the honest answer is that they worked together, as their letters show. But the Notes and their vision are hers.

What was that vision? She saw that the Engine worked on symbols, not merely numbers. She wrote that the Engine weaves algebraical patterns just as the Jacquard loom weaves flowers and leaves. And she suggested that, if the relations of musical sounds could be expressed in its notation, the Engine might compose elaborate pieces of music. She also wrote, with great good sense, that the Engine has no pretensions to originate anything: it can do whatever we know how to order it to perform. People still debate that remark about thinking machines.
Ada called her approach poetical science. She died in 1852, aged only thirty-six.
## Mr Babbage's temper

Babbage lived until 1871, increasingly bitter that his engines were never built. His engine was not shown at the Great Exhibition of 1851, which I visited as a young man, and he was much annoyed about it. He waged a famous war against the organ grinders and street musicians who played beneath his windows, and they, it seems, played all the louder for it.

He also left us a remark every teacher treasures. In his Passages from the Life of a Philosopher, of 1864, he wrote that on two occasions he had been asked, if you put into the machine wrong figures, will the right answers come out? And he said that he was not able rightly to apprehend the kind of confusion of ideas that could provoke such a question.
## A postscript from the future library

In the library of the future I read that, in 1991, the Science Museum in London completed a Difference Engine Number Two built to Babbage's later drawings, using only the precision of his era, and that it worked. I confess I put down the book and took a long sip of tea.
## Summary

Babbage designed the Difference Engine, which built tables by repeated addition, and the Analytical Engine, a general machine with a store, a mill, punched-card instructions and the power to choose. Lovelace's Notes of 1843 explained it, programmed it for Bernoulli numbers in Note G, and saw that it could handle symbols of any kind. Next time, back to the foothills: inequalities. Good night, my dear friend.

Ah, there you are, my dear friend. Mind the cat. Tonight I want to tell you about two men of my own century who did something remarkable: they took logic, which had belonged to philosophers since Aristotle, and made it into mathematics. Neither of them could have guessed that, a hundred years later, their algebra would run every computing machine in the world. I have that from the library of the future, and I still find it hard to believe.
## Augustus De Morgan

De Morgan was born in 1806 in Madurai, in India, where his father was an officer in the army of the East India Company. He lost the sight of one eye in infancy. He went up to Trinity College, Cambridge, and in 1827 he was Fourth Wrangler, which I note, without bitterness, is ten places better than fourteenth.

But he could not take a fellowship or a higher degree, because in those days Cambridge required you to sign the religious tests of the Church of England, and De Morgan, on principle, would not. So in 1828, aged only twenty-two, he became the first professor of mathematics at the new London University, now University College, in Gower Street, which admitted students regardless of religion. It is, as it happens, a short walk from my own lodgings in Bloomsbury, though I never had the honour of his acquaintance.

He was a man of principle to the point of stubbornness. He resigned his chair in 1831 over the college's treatment of a colleague, returned in 1836, and resigned again in 1866 over another matter of principle.
## De Morgan's gifts

He was a superb and witty teacher. He gave the name mathematical induction to a method of proof, in an article of 1838. He stated clearly the laws of logic that now bear his name, which you heard last time: not, A and B, is not A or not B. He helped found the London Mathematical Society in 1865 and was its first president. He taught Ada Lovelace by correspondence, and thought her very able indeed.

And he collected cranks. His book A Budget of Paradoxes, published in 1872, after his death, is a long, affectionate and very funny catalogue of people who claimed to have squared the circle and similar impossibilities. It contains his famous verse: great fleas have little fleas upon their backs to bite 'em, and little fleas have lesser fleas, and so ad infinitum.
You may remember his riddle from the lecture on minus times minus: I was x years old in the year x squared. He was forty-three in 1849, and forty-three squared is 1849.
## George Boole

Now to Lincoln. George Boole was born there in 1815, the son of John Boole, a shoemaker who loved science and instruments far more than shoes, which did his business no good. The family was poor. George had little formal schooling beyond the elementary. He taught himself Latin and Greek, then French, German and Italian, and then mathematics, from books.

At sixteen he was working as an assistant schoolmaster to support his family, and before he was twenty he had opened his own school. He read the great French mathematicians, Laplace and Lagrange, by candlelight after teaching all day. He began publishing papers, and in 1844 the Royal Society awarded him a gold medal for a paper on differential equations. Imagine it: a provincial schoolmaster without a degree, honoured by the Royal Society.
I have a particular fondness for Boole, because he was exactly the sort of person I spent twenty years teaching at the Mechanics' Institute: brilliant, untaught, and determined.
## The algebra of thought

In 1847, the same year De Morgan published his own book on formal logic, Boole published The Mathematical Analysis of Logic. His great insight was that the rules of reasoning behave like algebra, with symbols for classes of things.

Let x stand for all white things and y for all sheep. Then x times y stands for white sheep: things that are both. Multiplying means and. Now, what is x times x? White things that are white things: simply white things. So in Boole's algebra:
In ordinary arithmetic, that is true only for two numbers.
?? While I pour. Which two numbers equal their own squares?
=> Nought and one. Nought squared is nought, one squared is one.

And so Boole's algebra, read as true and false, works with just two values: one for true and nought for false. And is multiplication: one times one is one, true and true is true, but anything times nought is nought. Not x is one minus x.
## Cork and The Laws of Thought

In 1849, on the strength of his papers alone, Boole was appointed the first professor of mathematics at the new Queen's College, Cork, in Ireland. In 1854 he published his masterpiece, An Investigation of the Laws of Thought. He married Mary Everest, a niece of the George Everest after whom the mountain is named, and she became a thoughtful writer on teaching mathematics to children.

Boole died in 1864, aged only forty-nine, of a fever and pneumonia that followed a walk through heavy rain to his lectures. There is a story about how his wife nursed him which is often repeated, but it rests on thin evidence, and I shall not repeat it.
## The long afterlife

For decades Boole's algebra was admired as a curiosity. Then, in 1937, according to the library of the future, a young American engineer named Claude Shannon showed in his master's thesis that Boolean algebra describes electrical switching circuits exactly: a switch is on or off, one or nought, and switches in series make and, switches in parallel make or. Every computer since is built from circuits that do Boole's algebra, billions of times a second. Your little glass slate is, at heart, a very large and very fast Boolean argument.
## Summary

Augustus De Morgan, a man of principle and wit, was the first professor of mathematics at London University; he gave us De Morgan's laws, named induction and collected paradoxes. George Boole, self-taught son of a Lincoln shoemaker, turned logic into algebra, where x squared equals x and the only values are one and nought. Their work now runs every computer. Next time: what a proof is, and why mathematicians demand one. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. We stand at the foot of the summit. Before we climb, let me tell you about the two men who first reached it, by different routes, and then spent years quarrelling about who got there first.

I have a confession that bears on this. In my hall stand two umbrellas, named Newton and Leibniz. I have never been able to decide which I acquired first. Mrs Blewitt says it was Leibniz; I have a strong suspicion it was Newton. Tonight you will see why I have never dared to settle the matter.
## Newton

Isaac Newton was born at Woolsthorpe in Lincolnshire, on Christmas Day 1642, by the calendar then in use in England. His father had died before he was born. He went up to Trinity College, Cambridge. In 1665 the plague closed the university, and Newton went home to Woolsthorpe. In those two plague years, aged about twenty-three, he worked out the beginnings of the calculus, which he called the method of fluxions, his theory of colours, and the start of his ideas on gravitation.

The famous apple, I must say, is a story Newton himself told in old age to friends, including William Stukeley, who wrote it down. So an apple may well have fallen in the garden at Woolsthorpe and set him thinking. That it struck him on the head is a later embellishment.

In 1669 he became Lucasian Professor at Cambridge, the chair Mr Babbage would later hold. But he published very little of his calculus. He was secretive and hated controversy, having been bruised by arguments over his work on light.
## The Principia

In 1684 the astronomer Edmond Halley visited Newton to ask what path a planet would follow if the sun pulled on it with a force falling off as the square of the distance. Newton replied at once: an ellipse. He had calculated it. Halley urged him to publish, and the result, in 1687, was the Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica, the Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy, explaining the motions of planets, moons, comets and tides by one law of gravitation. Halley paid for the printing himself, since the Royal Society had spent its money on a book about the history of fishes. The Principia is written largely in the language of geometry, not of calculus, though calculus-like reasoning runs beneath it.

Newton later became Warden, and then Master, of the Royal Mint, where he pursued counterfeiters with great vigour, and President of the Royal Society. He died in 1727 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.
## Leibniz

Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz was born in Leipzig in 1646. He was a lawyer, diplomat, philosopher and courtier, and a mathematician of genius. He was in Paris on diplomatic business from 1672 to 1676, where the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens guided his study of mathematics. There, around 1675, he developed his own calculus.

He also built a calculating machine, the stepped reckoner, which could multiply, and showed a model to the Royal Society in London in 1673. He was an inventor of symbols: he understood that good notation does half the thinking for you. He wrote d x for a tiny difference in x, and a tall, stretched S, for summa, meaning sum, for adding up infinitely many tiny pieces: the integral sign. In 1684 he published his method, in a paper with a very long Latin title usually shortened to Nova Methodus, the new method. It was the first publication of the calculus.
## The quarrel

For some years all was courteous. Then Newton's supporters began to suggest that Leibniz had seen Newton's unpublished papers, or letters, and borrowed the idea. Leibniz's supporters returned the charge. In 1711 Leibniz appealed to the Royal Society for justice. The Society appointed a committee, which in 1712 reported in Newton's favour. The President of the Royal Society at the time was Newton, and historians have shown that he largely wrote the report himself.

The dispute damaged both men and, for a century, divided mathematicians. British mathematicians loyally used Newton's dot notation and fell behind the Continent, where Leibniz's notation flourished in the hands of the Bernoullis and Euler. In 1812, some years before I was born, young reformers at Cambridge, among them Mr Babbage and his friends in the Analytical Society, campaigned for Leibniz's d's; Babbage joked that they stood for the principles of pure d-ism, against the dot-age of the university. Leibniz died in 1716 in Hanover, rather neglected.
## The verdict of history
Historians today agree that both men discovered the calculus independently: Newton first, around 1665 and 1666, and Leibniz around 1675, publishing first. Both deserve the summit.
?? While I pour. Which of my umbrellas, then, came first?
=> I fear the honest answer is: Newton found the shop first, but Leibniz was first to tell anyone about it. And so they stand in the hall, and I shall not take sides.
## Summary

Newton developed fluxions in the plague years of 1665 and 1666, but published little; his Principia of 1687, paid for by Halley, explained the heavens. Leibniz developed calculus around 1675, published in 1684, and gave us d x and the integral sign. A bitter priority dispute followed, judged by a committee whose report Newton largely wrote. Both discovered it independently. Next, we begin the climb: the slope of a curve. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. We are halfway up the summit, and it is time to sit on a rock, pour some tea, and talk about the man whose fingerprints are on almost every page of it. You have heard his name in nearly every lecture lately. Tonight, Leonhard Euler himself.
## Basel

Euler was born in Basel, in Switzerland, in 1707, the son of a Protestant pastor who had himself studied mathematics. The young Euler was sent to the University of Basel, where the great Johann Bernoulli, the same who posed the brachistochrone, noticed his gifts and gave him private guidance on Saturday afternoons. His father wished him to become a pastor; Bernoulli persuaded the father otherwise. Every mathematician since owes Johann Bernoulli a debt for that conversation.
## St Petersburg and Berlin

In 1727 Euler went to the new Academy of Sciences in St Petersburg, founded by Peter the Great. There he lost the sight of his right eye, around 1738, after a fever. In 1741 he accepted the invitation of Frederick the Great to the Berlin Academy, where he stayed twenty-five years. Frederick, who preferred wit and French poetry, did not much care for the plain-spoken Swiss, and is reported to have called him a cyclops. In 1766 Euler returned to St Petersburg, at the invitation of Catherine the Great, and remained there until his death in 1783.
## Blindness

Soon after his return to Russia, a cataract took the sight of his remaining eye, and by 1771 he was almost completely blind. His output did not fall. It rose. He dictated to his sons and to assistants, working enormous calculations in his head with a memory that astonished everyone; it was said he could recite the whole of Virgil's Aeneid. Roughly half of his work was produced after 1765. I mention this with some feeling, my dear friend, because it shows beyond argument that mathematics does not live in the eyes. It lives in the mind, and it can be carried, held and turned over entirely by ear and memory.
## The Basel problem
Add up one, plus a quarter, plus a ninth, plus a sixteenth: one over each square number, for ever.

The total settles somewhere near one point six four five. What exactly? The best mathematicians of Europe, the Bernoullis among them, had tried and failed. In 1734 and 1735, Euler found it: pi squared over six. Pi, the number of circles, appearing in a sum about square numbers! It made his name across Europe. His first argument was daring rather than rigorous, and he spent years making it sound.
?? While I pour. Pi is about three point one four. Roughly what is pi squared over six?
=> Pi squared is just under ten, about nine point eight seven. Divided by six, about one point six four five.
## The bridges of Königsberg

The city of Königsberg, in Prussia, was built where a river divides around two islands, joined to the banks and to each other by seven bridges. The townsfolk wondered whether one could walk around the city crossing every bridge exactly once. In 1736 Euler proved it impossible. His reasoning ignored distances and shapes altogether: only which land areas are joined to which matters. Every time you pass through a piece of land, you use two bridges, one in and one out. So, except where the walk starts and finishes, every piece of land must touch an even number of bridges. In Königsberg, all four pieces of land touch an odd number. Impossible. This was the beginning of graph theory, and of topology, the geometry where shape matters but size does not.
## The notation

Euler gave us much of the language of mathematics. He introduced f of x for a function, in 1734. He used e for the exponential base. He used i for the square root of minus one, in 1777. He used the capital sigma for sums. And his widely read books made pi the standard symbol for the circle number. When you hear me say f of x, or e, or pi, you hear Euler.
## How much he wrote

Euler wrote more mathematics than anyone before or since: over eight hundred books and papers in his lifetime, and the St Petersburg Academy went on publishing his backlog for some fifty years after his death. The modern edition of his collected works runs to more than eighty large volumes. Pierre-Simon Laplace is reported to have told his students: read Euler, read Euler, he is the master of us all. The source for that remark is second-hand, but the sentiment was universal.
## A story I must disown

There is a famous tale that the French philosopher Diderot, visiting Catherine's court, annoyed everyone with his atheism, so Euler confronted him with a meaningless algebraic proof of the existence of God, and Diderot, ignorant of mathematics, fled back to France in confusion. It is a good story, and our own De Morgan helped to spread it. But historians regard it as almost certainly invented. Diderot was in fact a capable mathematician who had published papers on geometry and probability. I tell it only so that you may recognise it, and disbelieve it, when you meet it.
## The end

On the eighteenth of September 1783, Euler spent the morning calculating, discussed the newly discovered planet Uranus at lunch, and while playing with a grandchild suffered a stroke. As the Marquis de Condorcet put it in his eulogy, he ceased to calculate and to live.
## Summary

Euler, born in Basel in 1707, pupil of Johann Bernoulli, worked in St Petersburg and Berlin, and went nearly blind yet produced more than ever. He solved the Basel problem, founded graph theory with Königsberg's bridges, and gave us f of x, e, i and sigma. The Diderot story is a myth. Next, the second half of calculus: integrals. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight, a little gossip about three mathematicians of my own day, men whose names I heard spoken in the corridors of Cambridge and London as one might speak of cricketers. One of them carved an equation on a bridge; one was a lawyer who wrote mathematics in his lunch hour; and one was a poet with a temper. Between them they changed what algebra means.
## Hamilton

William Rowan Hamilton was born in Dublin in 1805. As a boy he was said to know a dozen languages, though the tale may have grown in the telling. While still an undergraduate at Trinity College Dublin, aged twenty-one, he was appointed Andrews Professor of Astronomy and, with it, Royal Astronomer of Ireland. He was a poor observer of stars, but a magnificent mathematician. He reformulated Newton's mechanics in a way that, the library of the future tells me, became essential to quantum physics a century later.
## The triplets

For years Hamilton tried to extend complex numbers, which describe points on a flat plane, to triplets of numbers that would describe three-dimensional space. He could add and subtract triplets, but he could not find a way to multiply and divide them that behaved. Years later he wrote to his son Archibald that, each morning that October, his sons would ask at breakfast: Well, Papa, can you multiply triplets? And he would sadly shake his head: No, I can only add and subtract them.
## Broom Bridge

On Monday the sixteenth of October 1843, Hamilton was walking with his wife along the Royal Canal in Dublin, on his way to a meeting of the Royal Irish Academy, when the answer came to him in a flash. Not triplets, but quadruplets: one real part and three imaginary units, i, j and k. He could not resist taking out his penknife and carving the formula into the stone of Broom Bridge.

In plain words: i squared equals j squared equals k squared equals i j k equals minus one. He called them quaternions. The carving has long since weathered away, but a plaque marks the spot, and mathematicians walk there every sixteenth of October to this day, I am informed.

The price of the discovery was startling. In quaternions, i times j is k, but j times i is minus k. The order of multiplication matters. Ever since childhood, everyone had assumed that a times b equals b times a. Hamilton showed that a perfectly good algebra could abandon that rule.
?? While I pour. Can you think of an everyday action where order matters: doing A then B differs from B then A?
=> Putting on socks then shoes, against shoes then socks. Or turning a book a quarter turn forward then sideways, against sideways then forward: try it, the results differ.
## Cayley

Arthur Cayley was born in 1821, and was Senior Wrangler at Cambridge in 1842: the top of the list. I, Fourteenth, used to look at his name with awe. Unable to find a mathematical post that paid, he became a barrister specialising in conveyancing: the dry legal business of property. He practised for fourteen years, and in that time, in the evenings and between deeds, he wrote around two hundred and fifty mathematical papers. In 1863 Cambridge at last created a chair for him, the Sadleirian professorship; he took a large drop in income to accept it, and never regretted it.

In 1858 Cayley published his memoir on the theory of matrices: square arrays of numbers that can be added and multiplied like single numbers, except that, as with quaternions, the order of multiplication matters. Matrices, the library tells me, are now the daily bread of engineers, physicists, economists, and the makers of computing machines.
## Sylvester

James Joseph Sylvester was born in London in 1814. He came second in the Cambridge examination of 1837, Second Wrangler, but as a Jew he could not sign the religious declaration then required, and so was refused his degree. Cambridge put that right only after the religious tests were abolished in 1871. He taught briefly at the University of Virginia, leaving after a few months following an ugly quarrel with a student; worked as an actuary; and studied law, which is how he met Cayley around 1847, at the Inns of Court. The two would walk around the courts talking about invariants: quantities that stay the same when you change your point of view. They remained friends and collaborators for life.

Sylvester loved inventing words. He coined matrix, in 1850, from the Latin word for womb, the thing from which other things are born. He also wrote poetry, and a book on the laws of verse. In 1876, aged sixty-one, he went to the new Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, where he built America's first serious school of mathematical research and founded the American Journal of Mathematics. In 1883, at sixty-eight, he returned to England as Savilian Professor of Geometry at Oxford.
## What they did

Between them, these three showed that algebra is not just arithmetic with letters. It is the study of any system of objects with operations that follow rules, and the rules can be chosen. Out of that idea came modern abstract algebra, and the algebra of matrices that runs half the machines of your century.
## Summary

Hamilton discovered quaternions on the sixteenth of October 1843, carving i squared equals j squared equals k squared equals i j k equals minus one on Broom Bridge, and showed that multiplication need not be commutative. Cayley, a lawyer for fourteen years, wrote about two hundred and fifty papers and created the algebra of matrices. Sylvester, denied his degree for his faith, coined the word matrix and founded research mathematics at Johns Hopkins. Next, a strange and wonderful result of the century after mine: Gödel's theorem. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight's lecture is on History of mathematics. It is a chapter from the history of our subject, full of real people and their quarrels. I have retold it in my own words from the Wikipedia article History of mathematics, written by a great many hands and shared under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licence. The facts are theirs, checked as carefully as I am able; the jokes, I am afraid, are mine.
Tonight, the whole history of our subject in one lecture. I shall go at a gallop, my dear friend, and hold on to your hat; most of the people I mention have lectures of their own.
## Beginnings

People counted long before they wrote. Notched bones, tallies and pebbles were among the first tools. Written mathematics appears with writing itself, in Mesopotamia and Egypt, about four thousand years ago and more. The Babylonians, on clay tablets, used a place-value system in base sixty, solved quadratic problems, and knew Pythagorean triples. The Egyptians, on papyrus, computed areas, volumes and shares, with unit fractions. Their mathematics was practical, for taxes, land, building and astronomy, and it was given as worked examples rather than general proofs.
## The Greeks

From about the sixth century before Christ, Greek thinkers began to ask why. Thales, so tradition says, and Pythagoras and his followers, began to prove general statements. Euclid's Elements, written around three hundred years before Christ in Alexandria, organised geometry and number theory as a chain of proofs from a few axioms, and became the most successful textbook in history. Archimedes found areas and volumes by methods close to calculus. Apollonius studied the conic sections. Later, Diophantus wrote on equations, Ptolemy on astronomy, and Hypatia taught in Alexandria until her murder in 415.
?? While I pour. What was new about Greek mathematics compared with Babylonian and Egyptian?
=> The Greeks emphasised general proofs from axioms, rather than worked examples and rules.
## China and India

Chinese mathematics developed independently. The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art, compiled over several centuries before and after the time of Christ, solves systems of equations by a method like elimination, and uses negative numbers. Later Chinese mathematicians computed pi with great accuracy. In India, mathematicians developed the decimal place-value system with nine digits and zero; Aryabhata, around 499, wrote on astronomy and arithmetic; Brahmagupta, in 628, gave rules for zero and negative numbers; and the Kerala school, from about 1400, found infinite series for sine, cosine and pi.
## The Islamic world

From the eighth century, scholars in Baghdad's House of Wisdom and across the Islamic world translated Greek and Indian works and went beyond them. Al-Khwarizmi, around 820, wrote the book that gave algebra its name. Omar Khayyam solved cubic equations geometrically. Others developed trigonometry, decimal fractions and much else. Through Spain and Sicily this learning passed to Europe.
## Europe awakens

Fibonacci's Liber Abaci of 1202 brought Hindu–Arabic numerals to Europe. In sixteenth-century Italy, Cardano and others solved cubic and quartic equations. Symbols arrived: Recorde's equals sign in 1557, Viète's letters for unknowns. In the seventeenth century, Descartes and Fermat joined algebra to geometry, Napier invented logarithms, Fermat and Pascal founded probability, and Newton and Leibniz invented the calculus.
## The eighteenth and nineteenth centuries

Euler, the most prolific of all, spread calculus everywhere. In my own century, Gauss transformed number theory; Cauchy and Weierstrass made calculus rigorous; Galois and Abel showed which equations can be solved by formulas; non-Euclidean geometry was discovered; Boole made logic algebraic; Cayley and Sylvester built matrices; Riemann reimagined geometry; and Cantor tamed the infinite.
## The twentieth century and after

Hilbert set the problems for a new century in 1900. Gödel showed the limits of proof; Turing defined computation; Emmy Noether reshaped algebra. Mathematics split into hundreds of fields, while computers opened new ones. Fermat's Last Theorem fell to Andrew Wiles in 1994; the Poincaré conjecture to Grigori Perelman in 2003. The library of the future tells me that more mathematics is now published each year than in whole centuries of the past.
## Summary

Mathematics began with counting, became written in Mesopotamia and Egypt, gained proof in Greece, place value and zero in India, algebra in the Islamic world, and calculus in seventeenth-century Europe. Since my own century it has grown into a vast, international enterprise.

That concludes my retelling of the Wikipedia article History of mathematics. My thanks to its many contributors; the full article, with its references, is on Wikipedia for anyone with a strong cup of tea.

Settle back, my friend, and let me tell you about Babylonian mathematics. It is a chapter from the history of our subject, full of real people and their quarrels. I have retold it in my own words from the Wikipedia article Babylonian mathematics, written by a great many hands and shared under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licence. The facts are theirs, checked as carefully as I am able; the jokes, I am afraid, are mine.
Tonight we travel to Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and the Euphrates, in what is now Iraq, where some of the oldest written mathematics in the world was pressed into wet clay with a reed.
## Clay and reed

The Babylonians wrote in cuneiform: wedge-shaped marks made by pressing the cut end of a reed into a tablet of damp clay. Clay, once dried or baked, lasts very well, and so hundreds of mathematical tablets survive, many from what is called the Old Babylonian period, roughly eighteen hundred to sixteen hundred years before Christ. Some were school exercises; I like to think of a bored pupil pressing wedges while the master paced.
## Base sixty

Their numbers used base sixty. We count in tens: units, tens, hundreds. They counted in sixties: units, sixties, sixty sixties, which is three thousand six hundred, and so on. Only two signs were needed, a wedge for one and a hooked mark for ten, combined to make every digit from one to fifty-nine. And it was a true place-value system: the same sign meant one, or sixty, or three thousand six hundred, according to its position. The idea of place value, which we met at base camp, appears here first.
?? While I pour. Why might sixty be a convenient base?
=> Because sixty divides evenly by two, three, four, five, six, ten, twelve, fifteen, twenty and thirty, so many fractions come out exactly.
## The missing zero

For a long time the Babylonians had no zero, so a reader had to guess from context whether a sign meant one, or sixty, or a sixtieth. Later, a separate sign came to be used as a placeholder between digits, though not at the end of a number, and not as a number in its own right. That last step was taken in India, as we heard in my lecture on zero.
## Square root of two

A famous small tablet in the Yale collection, known as YBC 7289, shows a square with its diagonals. Written along a diagonal is a number which, translated from base sixty, comes to about one point four one four two one three. The true square root of two is one point four one four two one three five six and so on. They had it correct to about six decimal places, nearly four thousand years ago. I have known Fellows of colleges who could not manage that after dinner.
## Problems and tables

The tablets contain multiplication tables, tables of reciprocals for doing division, and tables of squares. They contain problems we would now solve with quadratic equations, set as puzzles about fields and their sides, and solved by recipes equivalent to completing the square. And there is Plimpton 322, a tablet with a lecture of its own in our library, listing sets of numbers that fit the rule of Pythagoras, more than a thousand years before Pythagoras was born.
## Their legacy

The Babylonians also turned their arithmetic to the sky, and their astronomers made careful records and predictions. The Greeks borrowed their base sixty for astronomy, and so it comes down to us. Sixty seconds in a minute, sixty minutes in an hour and in a degree, three hundred and sixty degrees in a circle: every time you look at a clock, you are reading Babylonian.
## Summary

Babylonian scribes wrote mathematics on clay in cuneiform, in a place-value system of base sixty, at first without a zero. They tabulated reciprocals and squares, solved quadratic problems, found the square root of two to about six decimal places, and listed Pythagorean triples. Our minutes, seconds and degrees are their inheritance.

That concludes my retelling of the Wikipedia article Babylonian mathematics. My thanks to its many contributors; the full article, with its references, is on Wikipedia for anyone with a strong cup of tea.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight's lecture is on Ancient Egyptian mathematics. It is a chapter from the history of our subject, full of real people and their quarrels. I have retold it in my own words from the Wikipedia article Ancient Egyptian mathematics, written by a great many hands and shared under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licence. The facts are theirs, checked as carefully as I am able; the jokes, I am afraid, are mine.
Tonight we go up the Nile, to the mathematics that helped build the pyramids, survey fields after the floods, and pay the workers in bread and beer.
## Sources

Most of what we know comes from a handful of papyri. The greatest are the Rhind papyrus, which has its own lecture, and the Moscow papyrus, both from the Middle Kingdom period or copied from it, around four thousand years ago. There are also leather rolls, wooden boards and ostraca, which are broken bits of pottery used as scrap paper. The Egyptian scribes seem to have used mathematics chiefly for administration: grain, land, labour and building.
## Writing numbers

Egyptian numbers were decimal, like ours, but they did not use place value. Each power of ten had its own hieroglyph: a single stroke for one, a heel bone for ten, a coil of rope for a hundred, a lotus flower for a thousand, a raised finger for ten thousand, a tadpole for a hundred thousand, and for a million, a kneeling god with his arms raised, as if astonished by the size of the number. To write three hundred and twenty-four you drew three coils, two heel bones and four strokes.
?? While I pour. How many symbols would an Egyptian need to write nine hundred and ninety-nine?
=> Twenty-seven: nine coils, nine heel bones and nine strokes. Place value, with only three digits, is rather more economical.
## Multiplying and dividing

Multiplication worked by doubling, as I described in the Rhind lecture: double one number again and again, then add the rows whose multipliers make up the other number. Division was the same process in reverse: how many doublings of the divisor build up the dividend?
## Fractions

Egyptian fractions were unit fractions, with one on top, combined as sums: three quarters was written as a half plus a quarter. There was also a special sign for two thirds. Problems of sharing loaves among workers gave scribes plenty of practice.
## Geometry

The scribes could find areas of rectangles, triangles and trapeziums, and approximated the area of a circle well, as the Rhind lecture explains. The Moscow papyrus contains a jewel: the correct volume of a truncated pyramid, a pyramid with its top sliced off flat. It takes the heights and the two square sides, and combines them exactly as our modern formula does. How they found it, we do not know.
## Algebra of a kind

Some problems ask for an unknown quantity, which the scribes called aha, meaning a heap. A quantity and its seventh, together, make nineteen: what is the quantity? They solved such problems by a clever method of false position: guess a convenient answer, see how far wrong it comes out, and scale it.
?? Try it. Guess seven: seven and its seventh make eight. But we want nineteen. By what must we scale seven?
=> By nineteen eighths. Seven times nineteen eighths is a hundred and thirty-three eighths, sixteen and five eighths.
## Summary

Egyptian mathematics, known chiefly from the Rhind and Moscow papyri, used decimal hieroglyphs without place value, multiplied by doubling, wrote fractions as sums of unit fractions, and found areas and volumes, including the truncated pyramid. It was practical, ingenious and, in places, startlingly accurate.

That concludes my retelling of the Wikipedia article Ancient Egyptian mathematics. My thanks to its many contributors; the full article, with its references, is on Wikipedia for anyone with a strong cup of tea.

Next, a reading, which I have borrowed from the library of the future. It is called Ancient Greek mathematics. It is a chapter from the history of our subject, full of real people and their quarrels. I confess I have not yet found the time to retell this one in my own words, so the words are Wikipedia's, written by a great many hands, and I read them as faithfully as I can. I have adapted them only for listening: formulas are said in words, where a formula is displayed I add a short note in plain words, and now and then I interrupt with a remark of my own, which you will know by its frivolity. It is gentle going, hardly a number in sight.

Ancient Greek mathematics refers to the history of mathematical ideas and texts in Ancient Greece during classical and late antiquity, mostly from the 5th century BC to the 6th century AD. Greek mathematicians lived in cities spread around the shores of the ancient Mediterranean, from Anatolia to Italy and North Africa, but were united by Greek culture and the Greek language. The development of mathematics as a theoretical discipline and the systematization of the use of deductive reasoning and proofs is an important difference between Greek mathematics and those of preceding civilizations.

The early history of Greek mathematics is obscure, and traditional narratives of mathematical theorems found before the fifth century BC are regarded as later inventions. It is now generally accepted that treatises of deductive mathematics written in Greek began circulating around the mid-fifth century BC, but the earliest complete work on the subject is Euclid's Elements, written during the Hellenistic period. The works of renowned mathematicians Archimedes and Apollonius, as well as of the astronomer Hipparchus, also belong to this period. In the Imperial Roman era, Ptolemy used trigonometry to determine the positions of stars in the sky, while Nicomachus and other ancient philosophers revived ancient number theory and harmonics. During late antiquity, Pappus of Alexandria wrote his Collection, summarizing the work of his predecessors, while Diophantus' Arithmetica dealt with the solution of arithmetic problems by way of pre-modern algebra. Later authors such as Theon of Alexandria, his daughter Hypatia, and Eutocius of Ascalon wrote commentaries on the authors making up the ancient Greek mathematical corpus.

The works of ancient Greek mathematicians were copied in the Byzantine period and translated into Arabic and Latin, where they exerted influence on mathematics in the Islamic world and in Medieval Europe. During the Renaissance, the texts of Euclid, Archimedes, Apollonius, and Pappus in particular went on to influence the development of early modern mathematics. Some problems in Ancient Greek mathematics were solved only in the modern era by mathematicians such as Carl Gauss, and attempts to prove or disprove Euclid's parallel line postulate spurred the development of non-Euclidean geometry. Ancient Greek mathematics was not limited to theoretical works but was also used in other activities, such as business transactions and land mensuration, as evidenced by extant texts where computational procedures and practical considerations took more of a central role.
## Etymology

The Greek word mathēmatikē derives from máthēma, and ultimately from the verb manthánō. Strictly speaking, a máthēma could be any branch of learning, or anything learnt; however, since antiquity certain mathēmatá were granted special status: arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, and harmonics. These four mathēmatá, which appear listed together around the time of Archytas and Plato, would later become the medieval quadrivium. Geminus of Rhodes (1st century BC) later divided the mathematics of the quadrivium in two parts: one dealing with intelligibles (arithmetic and geometry), and the other with perceptibles (astronomy and harmonics). To the latter, he added mechanics, optics, geodesy, and logistics, which are now part of physics or applied mathematics.
## Origins

The origins of Greek mathematics are not well understood. The earliest advanced civilizations in Greece were the Minoan and later Mycenaean civilizations, both of which flourished in the second half of the Bronze Age. These civilizations possessed writing, including the Linear B script used by Mycenaean Greeks. The majority of Linear B tablets are administrative records, with many containing numerical quantities (including fractions and standardised measures), and some containing arithmetic. The mathematics from the preceding Babylonian and Egyptian civilizations were similarly focused on land mensuration and accounting. Although some problems were contrived to be challenging beyond any obvious practical application, there are no signs of explicit theoretical concerns as found in Ancient Greek mathematics. It is generally thought that Babylonian and Egyptian mathematics had an influence on the younger Greek culture, possibly through an oral tradition of mathematical problems over the course of centuries, though no direct evidence of transmission is available.

When Greek writing re-emerged in the 7th century BC, following the Late Bronze Age collapse, it was based on an entirely new system derived from the Phoenician alphabet, with Egyptian papyrus being the preferred medium. Because the earliest known mathematical treatises in Greek, starting with Hippocrates of Chios in the 5th century BC, have been lost, the early history of Greek mathematics must be reconstructed from information passed down through later authors, beginning in the mid-4th century BC. Much of the knowledge about early Greek mathematics is thanks to references by Plato, Aristotle, and from quotations of Eudemus of Rhodes' histories of mathematics by later authors. These references provide near-contemporary accounts for many mathematicians active in the 4th century BC. Euclid's Elements is also believed to contain many theorems that are attributed to mathematicians in the preceding centuries.
## Archaic period

Ancient Greek tradition attributes the origin of Greek mathematics to either Thales of Miletus (7th century BC), one of the legendary Seven Sages of Greece, or to Pythagoras of Samos (6th century BC), both of whom supposedly visited Egypt and Babylon and learned mathematics there. However, modern scholarship tends to be skeptical of such claims as neither Thales or Pythagoras left any writings that were available in the Classical period. Additionally, widespread literacy and the scribal culture that would have supported the transmission of mathematical treatises did not emerge fully until the 5th century; the oral literature of their time was primarily focused on public speeches and recitations of poetry. The standard view among historians is that the discoveries Thales and Pythagoras are credited with, such as Thales' Theorem, the Pythagorean theorem, and the Platonic solids, are the product of attributions by much later authors.
## Classical Greece

The earliest traces of Greek mathematical treatises appear in the second half of the fifth century BC. According to Eudemus, Hippocrates of Chios was the first to write a book of Elements in the tradition later continued by Euclid. Fragments from another treatise written by Hippocrates on lunes also survives, possibly as an attempt to square the circle. Eudemus' states that Hippocrates studied with an astronomer named Oenopides of Chios. Other mathematicians associated with Chios include Andron and Zenodotus, who may be associated with a "school of Oenopides" mentioned by Proclus.

Although many stories of the early Pythagoreans are likely apocryphal, including stories about people being drowned or exiled for sharing mathematical discoveries, some fifth-century Pythagoreans may have contributed to mathematics. Beginning with Philolaus of Croton, a contemporary of Socrates, studies in arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, and harmonics became increasingly associated with Pythagoreanism. Fragments of Philolaus' work are preserved in quotations from later authors. Aristotle is one of the earliest authors to associate Pythagoreanism with mathematics, though he never attributed anything specifically to Pythagoras.

Other extant evidence shows fifth-century philosophers' acquaintance with mathematics: Antiphon claimed to be able to construct a rectilinear figure with the same area as a given circle, while Hippias is credited with a method for squaring a circle with a neusis construction. Protagoras and Democritus debated the possibility for a line to intersect a circle at a single point. According to Archimedes, Democritus also asserted, apparently without proof, that the area of a cone was 1/3 the area of a cylinder with the same base, a result which was later proved by Eudoxus of Cnidus.
## Mathematics in the time of Plato

While Plato was not a mathematician, numerous early mathematicians were associated with Plato or with his Academy. Familiarity with mathematicians' work is also reflected in several Platonic dialogues where mathematics are mentioned, including the Meno, the Theaetetus, the Republic, and the Timaeus.

Archytas, a Pythagorean philosopher from Tarentum, was a friend of Plato who made several contributions to mathematics, including solving the problem of doubling the cube, now known to be impossible with only a compass and a straightedge, using an alternative method. He also systematized the study of means, and possibly worked on optics and mechanics. Archytas has been credited with early material found in Books VII–IX of the Elements, which deal with elementary number theory.

Theaetetus is one of the main characters in the Platonic dialogue named after him, where he works on a problem given to him by Theodorus of Cyrene to demonstrate that the square roots of several numbers from 3 to 17 are irrational, leading to the construction now known as the Spiral of Theodorus. Theaetetus is traditionally credited with much of the work contained in Book X of the Elements, concerned with incommensurable magnitudes, and Book XIII, which outlines the construction of the regular polyhedra. Although some of the regular polyhedra were certainly known previously, he is credited with their systematic study and the proof that only five of them exist.

Another mathematician who might have visited Plato's Academy is Eudoxus of Cnidus, associated with the theory of proportion found in Book V of the Elements. Archimedes credits Eudoxus with a proof that the volume of a cone is one-third the volume of a cylinder with the same base, which appears in two propositions in Book XII of the Elements. He also developed an astronomical calendar, now lost, that remains partially preserved in Aratus' poem Phaenomena. Eudoxus seems to have founded a school of mathematics in Cyzicus, where one of his students, Menaechmus, went on to develop a theory of conic sections.

## Hellenistic and early Roman period

Ancient Greek mathematics reached its acme during the Hellenistic and early Roman periods. Alexander the Great's conquest of the Eastern Mediterranean, Egypt, Mesopotamia, the Iranian plateau, Central Asia, and parts of India led to the spread of the Greek culture and language across these regions. Koine Greek became the lingua franca of scholarship throughout the Hellenistic world, and the mathematics of the Classical period merged with Egyptian and Babylonian mathematics to give rise to Hellenistic mathematics. Several centers of learning also appeared around this time, of which the most important one was the Mouseion in Alexandria, in Ptolemaic Egypt.

Although few in number, Hellenistic mathematicians actively communicated with each other in correspondence; publication consisted of passing and copying someone's work among colleagues. Much of the work represented by authors such as Euclid, Archimedes, Apollonius, and Ptolemy was of a very advanced level and rarely mastered outside a small circle.

Euclid collected many previous mathematical results and theorems in the Elements, a reference work that would become a canon of geometry and elementary number theory for many centuries. Archimedes used the method of exhaustion to approximate Pi (Measurement of a Circle), measured the surface area and volume of a sphere (On the Sphere and Cylinder), devised a mechanical method for developing solutions to mathematical problems using the law of the lever, (Method of Mechanical Theorems), and developed a way to represent very large numbers (The Sand-Reckoner). Apollonius of Perga, in his extant work Conics, refined and developed the theory of conic sections that was first outlined by Menaechmus, Euclid, and Conon of Samos. Trigonometry was developed around the time of the astronomer Hipparchus, and both trigonometry and astronomy were further developed by Ptolemy in his Almagest.
## Arithmetic

Euclid devoted part of his Elements (Books VII–IX) to topics that belong to elementary number theory, including prime numbers and divisibility. He gave an algorithm, the Euclidean algorithm, for computing the greatest common divisor of two numbers (Prop. VII.2) and a proof implying the infinitude of primes (Prop. IX.20). There is also older material likely based on Pythagorean teachings (Prop. Ancient Greek mathematicians conventionally separated numbers (mostly positive integers but occasionally rationals) from magnitudes or lengths, with only the former being the subject of arithmetic.

The Pythagorean tradition spoke of so-called polygonal or figurate numbers. The study of the sums of triangular and pentagonal numbers would prove fruitful in the early modern period. Building on the works of the earlier Pythagoreans, Nicomachus of Gerasa wrote an Introduction to Arithmetic which would go on to receive later commentary in late antiquity and the Middle Ages. Theon of Smyrna's Mathematics Useful For Understanding Plato, written around the same time, discusses the idea of congruences.

An epigram published by Lessing in 1773 appears to be a letter sent by Archimedes to Eratosthenes. The epigram proposed what has become known as Archimedes's cattle problem; its solution (absent from the manuscript) requires solving an indeterminate quadratic equation (which reduces to what would later be misnamed Pell's equation). As far as it is known, such equations were first successfully treated by Indian mathematicians. It is not known whether Archimedes himself had a method of solution.
## Geometry

During the Hellenistic age, three construction problems in geometry became famous: doubling the cube, trisecting an angle, and squaring the circle, all of which are now known to be impossible with a straight edge and compass. Many attempts were made using neusis constructions including the Cissoid of Diocles, Quadratrix, and the Conchoid of Nicomedes. Regular polygons and polyhedra had already been known before Euclid's Elements, but Archimedes extended their study to include semiregular polyhedra, also known as Archimedean solids. A work transmitted as Book XIV of Euclid's Elements, likely written a few centuries later by Hypsicles, lists other works on the topic, such Aristaeus the Elder's Comparison of Five Figures and Apollonius of Perga's Comparison of the Dodecahedron and the Icosahedron. Another book, transmitted as Book XV of Euclid's Elements, which was compiled in the 6th century AD, provides further developments.

Most of the works that became part of a standard mathematical curriculum in late antiquity were composed during the Hellenistic period: Data and Porisms by Euclid, several works by Apollonius of Perga including Cutting off a ratio, Cutting off an area, Determinate section, Tangencies, and Neusis, and several works dealing with loci, including Plane Loci and Conics by Apollonius, Solid Loci by Aristaeus the Elder, Loci on a Surface by Euclid, and On Means by Eratosthenes of Cyrene. All of these works other than Data, Conics Books I–VII, and Cutting off a ratio are lost but are known from Book 7 of Pappus' Collection.
## Applied mathematics

Astronomy was considered one of the mathēmatá, and accordingly many Hellenistic mathematicians devoted time to astronomy. The development of trigonometry as a synthesis of Babylonian and Greek methods is commonly attributed to Hipparchus, whose only extant work is his Commentary on the Phaenomena of Eudoxus and Aratus. In the 2nd century AD, Ptolemy wrote the Mathematical Syntaxis, now known as the Almagest, explaining the motions of the stars and planets according to a geocentric model, and calculated chord tables to a higher degree of precision, along with an instruction manual, in the Handy Tables.

The ancient Greeks regarded harmonics as the science of the arrangements of pitched sounds behind musical melody, including the principles which govern them. It was the most important branch of ancient Greek musical theory, studied by philosophers, mathematicians and astronomers as well as by musical specialists. Works in mathematical harmonics in the Hellenistic period include the Sectio Canonis, attributed to Euclid, and Ptolemy's Harmonics.

The study of optics was often viewed as a part of applied geometry. An extant work on catoptrics is dubiously attributed to Euclid. Archimedes presumably wrote a now lost work on catoptrics, while Diocles' On Burning Mirrors is extant in Arabic. Mechanics was considered a subordinate science to geometry, similar to optics, and the first mathematical treatment of mechanical topics appears in the Aristotelian Mechanical Problems. Other works in this tradition include Archimedes' On the Equilibrium of Planes, Philo's Compendium of Mechanics, and Hero's Mechanica (extant in Arabic). The construction of analogue computers like the Antikythera mechanism, the measurement of the circumference of the Earth by Eratosthenes, and the design of sundials and water clocks by Ctesibius and others are additional examples of applied mathematics in this period.
## Late antiquity

Although the mathematicians in the later Roman era generally had few notable original works, they are distinguished for their commentaries and expositions on the works of their predecessors. These commentaries have preserved valuable extracts from works no longer extant, or historical allusions which, in the absence of original documents, are precious because of their rarity.
## Diophantus' Arithmetica

Diophantus, arguably active no later than the 3rd century AD, wrote a book on polygonal numbers in addition to a work in pre-modern algebra, the Arithmetica. It is a collection of 290 algebraic problems giving numerical solutions of determinate equations (those with a unique solution) and indeterminate equations (which admit of more than one solution). Arithmetica was originally written in thirteen books, but only six of them survive in Greek, while another four books survive in Arabic, which were discovered in 1968. The books in Arabic correspond to books 4 to 7 of the original treatise, while the Greek books correspond to books 1 to 3 and 8 to 10. Diophantus made use of pre-modern algebraic symbolism in the form of an abridged notation for frequently occurring operations, and an abbreviation for the unknown number or arithmos (zeta) as well as for the powers of the unknown.
## Pappus' Collection

Pappus of Alexandria compiled a survey of earlier mathematical methods and results in the Collection in eight books, of which part of Book II and Books III–VII are extant in Greek and Book VIII is extant in Arabic. The collection covers a wide span of Ancient Greek mathematics, with a particular focus on the Hellenistic period. Book III is framed as a letter to Pandrosion, a woman mathematician, and discusses solutions to three construction problems: doubling the cube, angle trisection, and squaring the circle. Book IV discusses classical geometry, which Pappus divides into plane geometry, line geometry, and solid geometry, and includes a discussion of Archimedes' construction of the arbelos. Book V discusses isoperimetric figures, summarizing otherwise lost works by Zenodotus and Archimedes on isoperimetric plane and solid figures, respectively. Book VI deals with astronomy, commenting on some of the works making up the Little Astronomy. Book VII deals with ancient analysis, providing epitomes and lemmas from otherwise lost works of Apollonius and others. Book VIII is an introduction to ancient mechanics. The Greek version breaks off in the middle of a sentence discussing Hero of Alexandria, but a complete edition of Book VIII survives in Arabic.
## Mathematical commentaries

The commentary tradition began in the late Hellenistic period and continued into late antiquity. The first known commentary on the Elements was written by Hero of Alexandria, who likely set the format for future commentaries. Serenus of Antinoöpolis wrote a lost commentary on the Conics of Apollonius, along with two works that survive, Section of a Cylinder and Section of a Cone, expanding on specific subjects in the Conics. Pappus wrote a commentary on Book X of the Elements, while Heliodorus of Larissa wrote a summary of Euclid's Optics.

Many of the late antique commentators were associated with Neoplatonist philosophy. These include Porphyry of Tyre, a student of Plotinus, who wrote a commentary on Ptolemy's Harmonics, and Iamblichus, a student of Porphyry, who wrote a commentary on Nicomachus' Introduction to Arithmetic. Proclus, active in 5th-century Athens, wrote a commentary on Euclid's Elements, of which the first book survives, while his contemporary Domninus of Larissa wrote a Manual of Introductory Arithmetic, combining ideas from Nicomachus' and Euclid's number theory. Marinus of Neapolis, Proclus' successor, wrote an Introduction to Euclid's Data.

In Alexandria, Theon of Alexandria wrote a commentary on Ptolemy's Almagest and two commentaries on the Handy Tables, while his daughter Hypatia possibly wrote a commentary on Diophantus' Arithmetica and a commentary on the Conics of Apollonius, neither of which have survived. Ammonius Hermiae, John Philoponus, and Simplicius of Cilicia wrote commentaries on the works of Aristotle that preserve information on earlier mathematicians and philosophers. Eutocius of Ascalon (around 480–540), a student of Ammonius, wrote a commentary on Apollonius' Conics and commentaries on treatises of Archimedes that are extant.

The commentary tradition continued elsewhere in the Byzantine era. Anthemius of Tralles wrote a work On Surprising Mechanisms which treats "burning mirrors" and skeptically attempts to explain the function of Archimedes' heat ray. Isidore of Miletus, who took over construction of the Hagia Sophia after Anthemius' death, supervised the revision of Eutocius' commentaries of Archimedes. From someone in Isidore's circle we also have a work on polyhedra that is transmitted as Book XV of Euclid's Elements. In Rome, Boethius translated works on the quadrivium into Latin, deriving much of his commentary from Nicomachus' Introduction to Arithmetic and Introduction to Harmonics.
